subject: Science
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 45 minutes × 8 periods = 360 minutes
Total: 8 periods · 6h 0min

periods.stage_label: Observe and describe components of a habitat
periods.activity_title: Mapping What Lives Where — Biotic and Abiotic in Two Habitats
periods.activity_description: Students examine two contrasting habitat cards (pond and forest) and record all observable biotic and abiotic components in a two-column table. They identify how different organisms in the same habitat use resources differently, such as a nocturnal snake and a diurnal rodent sharing a forest.

roles.role_description: Distributes habitat cards, poses guiding questions about what organisms need to survive, and leads a brief whole-class share-out after independent work.
Complete the two-column table for each habitat card, listing biotic and abiotic components and noting one example of shared-but-differentiated resource use.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the chapter's central question — how do living things and their environments hold together — and distributes habitat cards for the pond and forest.
Students individually examine each card and populate a biotic-abiotic table, adding a brief note on one example of two organisms sharing the same habitat differently.
Whole-class share-out: teacher calls on pairs of students to name one biotic and one abiotic component from each habitat and records responses on the board.
Teacher consolidates by defining habitat, biotic, and abiotic formally, connecting student responses to the textbook terms.

periods.teacher_notes: This opening unit orients students to the chapter's foundational vocabulary before any abstract concepts are introduced; resist moving to definitions until students have generated their own observations. A common early error is treating sunlight and temperature as living things because organisms 'need' them — press students to distinguish between what an organism needs and what the organism itself is. If students finish the table quickly, ask them to identify one organism that could not survive if a single abiotic component were removed, as a preview of what is coming in later units.

periods.stage_label: Observe and describe components of a habitat
periods.activity_title: Counting Communities — A 1 m² Sampling Activity
periods.activity_description: Student groups mark a 1 m × 1 m area in the school garden or a nearby patch, systematically count and record every plant and animal species present, and use their data to distinguish between the concepts of population and community as they emerge from real observation.

roles.role_description: Guides groups in marking their plot, prompts systematic counting, and facilitates the debrief that connects field data to the formal definitions of population and community.
Mark and survey the plot, record species counts in a shared table, and identify which entries constitute populations and which together form a community.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reviews biotic-abiotic learning from the previous unit and explains the task — groups will survey a small real area to find actual populations.
Groups move to their plots, mark the boundary, and carefully count and record each distinct plant and animal species alongside the number of individuals observed.
Back in the classroom, groups compare their tables: teacher asks what they call all the individuals of one species in their plot, then what they call the whole collection of species together.
Teacher formalises the terms population and community using student data as the concrete referent, then asks groups to write one sentence distinguishing the two using their own plot data.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit builds directly on the habitat vocabulary established in the previous unit by grounding population and community in first-hand counts rather than definitions. A frequent confusion is treating population and community as synonyms — use the groups' own data to make the distinction tangible: all the ants in the plot are one population, but ants plus grass plus beetles together are the community. If outdoor access is not possible, provide a detailed illustration of a marked garden plot with species counts as a substitute.
materials: String or chalk for marking 1 m × 1 m plot

periods.stage_label: Classify interactions and construct feeding relationships
periods.activity_title: Who Interacts with Whom? Sorting Ecosystem Interactions
periods.activity_description: Students read a diagram of a pond habitat and classify each visible interaction as biotic-abiotic, abiotic-abiotic, or biotic-biotic. They also distinguish producers, herbivores, carnivores, and omnivores from the pond organisms shown, building a foundational classification of ecosystem roles.

roles.role_description: Poses the sorting challenge, circulates to probe student reasoning for each classification, and leads a structured discussion to surface and correct misclassifications.
Examine the pond diagram, classify each interaction into the three categories, and annotate each organism with its feeding role.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the ecosystem definition by connecting community and habitat from the previous two units, then presents the pond diagram and poses the sorting challenge.
Groups examine the diagram and classify each interaction, writing the category and a one-phrase justification next to each arrow or relationship shown.
Groups share their classifications; teacher records disagreements on the board and facilitates inquiry: what criterion separates biotic-biotic from biotic-abiotic?
Students individually annotate each organism in the diagram as producer, herbivore, carnivore, or omnivore, preparing for food-chain work in the next unit.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit moves students from describing components to classifying the relationships between them — a meaningfully higher cognitive demand than the first two units. A predictable error is classifying a plant absorbing sunlight as a biotic-biotic interaction because the plant is living; redirect attention to the nature of both parties in the interaction, not just one. The individual annotation at the close of this unit is an informal checkpoint: students who correctly label producers versus consumers are ready for the food-chain construction in the next unit.
materials: Printed pond habitat diagram (with interaction arrows)

periods.stage_label: Classify interactions and construct feeding relationships
periods.activity_title: Building Food Chains and Webs — From Grassland to Crop Field
periods.activity_description: Students construct a linear food chain from a grassland organism set (grass, grasshopper, frog, snake, eagle), assign each organism its trophic level, then extend the task by completing a partial food web by adding missing feeding arrows, recognising that most organisms participate in multiple chains simultaneously.

roles.role_description: Introduces trophic levels using the chain students construct, then distributes the partial food web and guides groups to identify which feeding relationships are missing.
Arrange organism cards into a food chain, label trophic levels, then draw missing arrows into the food web diagram and write one sentence explaining why a web is a more accurate picture than a chain.

time_bands.activity: Teacher revisits the producer-consumer classification from the previous unit and introduces food chain as a formalisation of feeding direction.
Groups arrange grassland organism cards into a food chain, draw the chain with directional arrows, and label each position with its trophic level number.
Teacher introduces the partial food web diagram; groups identify missing feeding relationships and add arrows, then verify their web against the completed chain.
Each group writes one sentence explaining the difference between a food chain and a food web using their own diagram as evidence.

periods.teacher_notes: Building on the classification work of the previous unit, this unit asks students to construct rather than merely sort — a step up in cognitive demand. A common error is reversing the arrow direction in a food chain, treating it as pointing from predator to prey; reinforce that the arrow follows the flow of energy or matter, pointing from what is eaten to what eats it. Groups that finish early can be asked to identify which organism in their web would cause the greatest disruption if removed, which anticipates the cascading-consequences reasoning of the next stage.
materials: Grassland organism cards (grass, grasshopper, frog, snake, eagle)

periods.stage_label: Explain causal mechanisms — decomposers, competition, and mutualism
periods.activity_title: Beyond Feeding: Decomposers and the Full Cast of Relationships
periods.activity_description: Students learn why decomposers are essential to nutrient cycling, then distinguish mutualism, commensalism, and parasitism through concrete examples from the chapter. They produce a relationship summary chart that maps each inter-organism interaction type to its defining feature and a chapter example.

roles.role_description: Explains decomposition and nutrient return using the mushroom-on-dead-tree and dung-beetle examples, then leads the class through mutualism, commensalism, and parasitism with targeted questioning.
Record each relationship type in a summary chart with its defining feature and chapter example, then write one sentence explaining why competition regulates population size.

time_bands.activity: Teacher asks where dead organisms go in the food web students built in the previous unit, then explains the role of decomposers using mushroom and dung-beetle examples from the chapter.
Teacher presents mutualism (honeybee-flower), commensalism (orchid on tree), and parasitism (tick on dog), pausing after each for students to write the defining feature and example in their chart.
Teacher explains competition for resources (food, water, space, sunlight) and how it regulates population size; students add competition to their chart and write the explanatory sentence.
Quick pair-check: each student reads their competition sentence to a partner, and pairs flag any sentence that does not include the word 'regulate' or 'balance' for class correction.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit introduces the causal mechanisms that sustain ecosystem balance, building on the feeding relationships established in the two previous units. A frequent misconception is treating commensalism as mutualism because 'the tree doesn't mind' — press students to distinguish no effect from benefit, not just the direction of benefit. The pair-check at the close is a fast formative checkpoint: if most sentences lack causal language, spend an extra moment before moving on to the next unit.
materials: Relationship summary chart template (four rows: decomposition, mutualism, commensalism, parasitism, competition)

periods.stage_label: Analyse cascading consequences of ecosystem disruption
periods.activity_title: The Frog Leg Export Ban — Tracing a Cascade
periods.activity_description: Students read the historical case of India's frog leg export in the 1980s and map the chain of consequences step by step: reduced frog populations, increased agricultural pests, synthetic pesticide overuse, and eventual government ban. They then construct a parallel cascade for the pond-pollution plant-death scenario and compare the two chains.

roles.role_description: Sets up the reading task, poses the core inquiry question — what triggered the government ban and why — and facilitates comparison of the two cascade chains.

Read the frog case study, map the cascade as a sequence of linked consequences, then construct a second cascade from the pond-pollution scenario and identify one structural similarity between the two chains.

time_bands.activity: Teacher recalls the concept of ecosystem balance from the previous unit and poses the inquiry question: what happens when one organism in a food web is suddenly removed at scale?
Groups read the frog leg export case study and map the cascade as a step-by-step chain, with an arrow connecting each consequence to the next.
Groups construct a second cascade chain for the pond-pollution scenario (plant death → oxygen drop → fish die → insect rise → pesticide use) alongside the frog chain.
Groups compare the two chains and write one sentence naming one structural feature that both cascades share, then share with the class for discussion.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit marks the shift from explaining mechanisms to analysing how disruptions propagate through entire systems — the highest-demand work in the arc so far. A common error is listing consequences in isolation rather than as a chain where each step causes the next; encourage students to draw explicit arrows between steps rather than bullet points. Groups that identify that both cascades involve a population reduction triggering a trophic imbalance are demonstrating the kind of pattern recognition this stage targets.
materials: Printed frog leg export case study (Activity 12.9 text)

periods.stage_label: Analyse cascading consequences of ecosystem disruption
periods.activity_title: Fish in the Pond — Tracing Indirect Effects Across Biotic and Abiotic Components
periods.activity_description: Students read and analyse the research study comparing two ponds — one with fish and one without — and trace how fish presence caused indirect effects on dragonfly populations, then pollinator populations, and finally on seed production in nearby plants, mapping the full biotic-abiotic web of consequences.

roles.role_description: Introduces the two-pond study, prompts students to predict effects before they read, and facilitates analysis of why the consequences crossed from aquatic to terrestrial systems.
Predict the effect of adding fish to a pond on land plants, read the study to check their prediction, map the full indirect chain, and identify which links cross the aquatic-terrestrial boundary.

time_bands.activity: Teacher presents the two-pond setup and asks groups to predict: if fish are added to a pond, what might happen to seed production in a meadow 50 metres away? Groups record predictions.
Groups read the two-pond study and map the complete chain: fish eat dragonfly larvae → fewer dragonflies → more bees and butterflies → greater seed production near the pond with fish.
Groups compare their prediction to the actual chain, annotate each link as biotic-biotic or biotic-abiotic, and identify the two links that cross the aquatic-terrestrial boundary.
Whole-class discussion: teacher asks why this cascade is harder to predict than the frog case, linking the answer to the concept of indirect effects introduced in the previous unit.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit deepens the cascading-consequences analysis from the previous unit by introducing indirect effects that cross ecosystem boundaries — a conceptually harder step. Students who predicted only direct effects (fish eat dragonflies, fewer dragonflies) without anticipating the pollinator and seed-production links are revealing exactly the gap this unit is designed to close. Encourage annotation of boundary-crossing links in a different colour to make the aquatic-terrestrial transition visible.
homework: Choose one ecosystem mentioned in the chapter (Sundarbans, a local river, or your school garden). Write a short paragraph predicting one cascade of consequences if a single species were removed from it, using the chain-arrow format from the unit.

periods.stage_label: Evaluate ecosystem health and the consequences of human disruption
periods.activity_title: The Sundarbans and the Green Revolution — Reading Disruption at Scale
periods.activity_description: Students examine the Sundarbans case study and the Green Revolution narrative to evaluate how large-scale human actions disrupt ecosystem relationships, using evidence from both cases to argue whether a disrupted ecosystem can recover naturally or always requires human intervention.

roles.role_description: Frames the evaluative question, provides guiding prompts for reading both case studies, and facilitates the structured argument session at the close.
Read both case studies, map the human action and its ecosystem consequences in each, and construct a written argument with evidence responding to the recovery question.

time_bands.activity: Teacher connects the cascade analysis from the previous two units to the question of scale: what happens when disruption is not a single export policy but decades of farming practice or ongoing deforestation?
Groups read the Sundarbans section and the Green Revolution narrative, recording for each: the human action, the ecosystem relationship disrupted, and the consequence traced in the text.
Groups use their evidence to draft a written argument responding to the question: does the Sundarbans or Green Revolution case suggest ecosystems can recover without human intervention, and why?

Two groups share contrasting arguments; teacher facilitates discussion linking both cases to the chapter's central idea that disruptions cascade through the full web of biotic and abiotic relationships.

periods.teacher_notes: This closing unit asks students to evaluate rather than only trace — using case-study evidence to construct and defend a position — which is the highest cognitive demand of the arc. A predictable weakness is arguments that list facts without connecting them causally to the recovery question; push students to link each piece of evidence to the claim using a 'because' or 'therefore'. The final discussion deliberately surfaces disagreement between groups, so do not resolve it too quickly — the productive tension between the two cases is itself the lesson.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Observe and describe components of a habitat
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students observe and record biotic and abiotic components of two contrasting habitats and conduct a real plot survey to distinguish populations from communities through direct observation.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can identify and record the biotic and abiotic components of a given habitat and use observational data to distinguish between a population and a community.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Classify interactions and construct feeding relationships
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students classify ecosystem interactions into biotic-biotic, biotic-abiotic, and abiotic-abiotic categories, then construct food chains, assign trophic levels, and complete a food web by identifying missing feeding relationships.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can classify interactions among ecosystem components by type and construct an accurate food chain and food web, labelling trophic levels and explaining why a web better represents feeding relationships than a single chain.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Explain causal mechanisms — decomposers, competition, and mutualism
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students explain the causal role of decomposers in nutrient cycling and distinguish mutualism, commensalism, parasitism, and competition by mapping each to its defining mechanism and a chapter example.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can explain why decomposers are essential to ecosystem function and distinguish among mutualism, commensalism, parasitism, and competition by identifying the defining benefit-harm relationship in each, with a supporting example from the chapter.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Analyse cascading consequences of ecosystem disruption
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students read and analyse two case studies — the frog leg export and the two-pond fish study — to trace how a single change to one population triggers a chain of indirect consequences across biotic and abiotic components and across ecosystem boundaries.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can trace and explain how a single disruption to one population causes a cascade of indirect consequences through a food web, identifying which links cross biotic-abiotic or aquatic-terrestrial boundaries.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Evaluate ecosystem health and the consequences of human disruption
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students evaluate two large-scale human disruptions — deforestation in the Sundarbans and Green Revolution farming practices — using case-study evidence to construct and defend an argument about whether disrupted ecosystems can recover naturally.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can use evidence from real ecosystem case studies to evaluate how large-scale human actions disrupt the full web of biotic and abiotic relationships, and construct a reasoned argument about the conditions under which recovery is possible.

assessment_items.stage_label: Observe and describe components of a habitat
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can identify and record the biotic and abiotic components of a given habitat and use observational data to distinguish between a population and a community.

competency.competency_text: Analyses patterns of relationships between living organisms and their environments in terms of dependence on and response to each other.

assessment_items.question_text: A student surveys a small pond and records the following: 14 frogs of the same species, 6 water lily plants, 3 species of algae, and direct sunlight falling on the water surface. Which statement correctly uses these observations to distinguish a population from a community?

options.label: A
options.text: All organisms recorded — frogs, water lilies, and algae — together form a single large population of the pond.

options.label: B
options.text: The 14 frogs form a population; all the frogs, water lilies, algae, and sunlight together form the community.

options.label: C
options.text: The 14 frogs form a population; all the frogs, water lilies, and algae together form the community.

options.label: D
options.text: The 14 frogs form the community because they share the same habitat; each plant species is a separate population.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Indicates the student has not yet separated biotic from abiotic components — sunlight is included in what should be a biotic-only community list, suggesting confusion between habitat and community.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Reveals a collapse of the population-community distinction: the student treats all organisms in the habitat as a single population rather than recognising that a population requires same-species membership.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Shows a reversal of the two terms — the student applies 'community' to a same-species group and reserves 'population' for individual plant species, inverting the correct definitions.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who struggle with reading-heavy stems can be asked to draw or label the survey data before selecting an option. Oral administration — reading the stem aloud and asking students to point to the correct statement — is equally valid.

assessment_items.stage_label: Observe and describe components of a habitat
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can identify and record the biotic and abiotic components of a given habitat and use observational data to distinguish between a population and a community.

competency.competency_text: Analyses patterns of relationships between living organisms and their environments in terms of dependence on and response to each other.

assessment_items.question_text: In a forest habitat, which of the following is correctly identified as an abiotic component?

options.label: A
options.text: A mushroom growing on a dead tree trunk.

options.label: B
options.text: A nocturnal snake resting under leaf litter.

options.label: C
options.text: Microorganisms living in the topsoil.

options.label: D
options.text: Soil temperature near the forest floor.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Selecting the mushroom suggests the student has not yet learned that decomposers, though non-plant and non-animal, are still biotic — a common surprise at this stage.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Selecting the snake may reflect the misconception that 'abiotic' means 'inactive' or 'hidden' — the snake is nocturnal and unseen during the day, leading some students to categorise it as non-living.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Selecting microorganisms reveals the same misconception as option A — students who associate 'living thing' only with visible organisms may not classify microscopic organisms as biotic.

MCQ.inclusivity: For students with language difficulties, the question can be presented with small icons beside each option. Asking students to sort the four options into a biotic-abiotic two-column table before selecting is also a valid scaffold.

assessment_items.stage_label: Classify interactions and construct feeding relationships
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can classify interactions among ecosystem components by type and construct an accurate food chain and food web, labelling trophic levels and explaining why a web better represents feeding relationships than a single chain.

competency.competency_text: Analyses patterns of relationships between living organisms and their environments in terms of dependence on and response to each other.

assessment_items.question_text: In a grassland food chain — Grass → Grasshopper → Frog → Snake → Eagle — a student labels the frog as occupying the second trophic level. Which statement correctly evaluates this labelling?

options.label: A
options.text: The labelling is correct because the frog eats only one type of organism.

options.label: B
options.text: The labelling is correct because the frog is a carnivore and all carnivores occupy the second trophic level.

options.label: C
options.text: The labelling is incorrect; the frog occupies the third trophic level because it is the second consumer in the chain.

options.label: D
options.text: The labelling is incorrect; trophic levels only apply to producers and top predators, not intermediate organisms.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Reveals that the student is counting the frog's diet choices rather than counting its position in the chain — a confusion between dietary breadth and trophic position.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Suggests the student holds a misconception that trophic levels are a binary concept (producers vs. top predators) rather than a positional numbering applied to every organism in the chain.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Reveals a generalisation error: the student has formed a rule that 'carnivore = second trophic level', ignoring that carnivores can occupy different levels depending on their chain position.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students can be asked to draw the chain with numbered positions before answering, making the counting process explicit. Pair discussion before individual selection is also effective for students who need to externalise their reasoning.

assessment_items.stage_label: Classify interactions and construct feeding relationships
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can classify interactions among ecosystem components by type and construct an accurate food chain and food web, labelling trophic levels and explaining why a web better represents feeding relationships than a single chain.

competency.competency_text: Analyses patterns of relationships between living organisms and their environments in terms of dependence on and response to each other.

assessment_items.visual_stimulus:
Interaction | Component 1 | Component 2
P | Plant roots | Soil (prevents erosion) | 
Q | Snake | Rodent |
R | Sunlight | Water (drives evaporation) |
S | Fish | Water oxygen levels |
assessment_items.question_text: Refer to the table provided. Which row shows a biotic-abiotic interaction?

options.label: A
options.text: Row P only.

options.label: B
options.text: Row Q only.

options.label: C
options.text: Row R only.

options.label: D
options.text: Rows P and S.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Selecting only Row P suggests the student recognises one biotic-abiotic pair but misses Row S — possibly because 'oxygen levels' sounds like a biological outcome and the student does not classify dissolved oxygen as an abiotic component.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Selecting Row Q reveals confusion between biotic-biotic and biotic-abiotic: snake eating a rodent involves two living organisms and is biotic-biotic, not biotic-abiotic.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Selecting Row R shows the student recognises an abiotic-abiotic interaction (sunlight driving evaporation of water) but misclassifies it as biotic-abiotic, possibly because sunlight supports life.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students can be asked to annotate each row with B (biotic) or A (abiotic) next to each component before classifying the interaction type. Visual learners benefit from colour-coding biotic and abiotic components across the table.

assessment_items.stage_label: Classify interactions and construct feeding relationships
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can classify interactions among ecosystem components by type and construct an accurate food chain and food web, labelling trophic levels and explaining why a web better represents feeding relationships than a single chain.

competency.competency_text: Analyses patterns of relationships between living organisms and their environments in terms of dependence on and response to each other.

assessment_items.question_text: A student draws a single food chain for a grassland: Grass → Grasshopper → Frog → Snake → Eagle. A classmate argues that this chain is not a complete picture of the grassland's feeding relationships because a frog also eats beetles and a snake also eats rodents. Using these additional relationships, explain why a food web is a more accurate representation than a single food chain, and draw or describe the additional arrows needed.
expected_elements: Identifies that a food web connects multiple food chains, allowing one organism to appear in more than one feeding relationship.
Correctly identifies at least one additional chain that branches from the original (e.g. Grass → Beetle → Frog or Rodent → Snake).
States that a food web is more accurate because real organisms have multiple food sources or multiple predators, which a single chain cannot show.
Represents the additional relationships with directional arrows or a clear verbal description of the direction of energy/matter flow.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who find drawing difficult can describe the additional arrows verbally in full sentences. For students who need a scaffold, provide a blank web template with the original five organisms already placed and ask them to add branches.

assessment_items.stage_label: Explain causal mechanisms — decomposers, competition, and mutualism
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can explain why decomposers are essential to ecosystem function and distinguish among mutualism, commensalism, parasitism, and competition by identifying the defining benefit-harm relationship in each, with a supporting example from the chapter.

competency.competency_text: Analyses patterns of relationships between living organisms and their environments in terms of dependence on and response to each other.

assessment_items.question_text: Mushrooms are frequently observed growing on dead trees during the rainy season. Which statement best explains the role these mushrooms play in the ecosystem?

options.label: A
options.text: Mushrooms are consumers that compete with other organisms for the dead tree as a food source.

options.label: B
options.text: Mushrooms are decomposers that break down complex substances in the dead tree into simpler ones, returning nutrients to the soil.

options.label: C
options.text: Mushrooms are in a mutualistic relationship with the tree, providing nutrients in exchange for shelter.

options.label: D
options.text: Mushrooms are producers that use dead wood as a surface to access sunlight for photosynthesis.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Selecting 'producer' reveals the misconception that all non-animal organisms that grow on surfaces must photosynthesise — the student has not yet distinguished fungi from plants.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Selecting 'consumer' shows that the student places decomposers inside the consumer category rather than recognising them as a distinct functional group that processes dead organic matter.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Selecting 'mutualistic relationship' reveals confusion about two things simultaneously: the tree is dead (so no relationship is active), and mutualism requires both parties to be alive and benefiting.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students can be shown an image of mushrooms on a dead log and asked to circle what is alive and what is not before selecting an answer. This grounds the question in observation before requiring classification.

assessment_items.stage_label: Explain causal mechanisms — decomposers, competition, and mutualism
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can explain why decomposers are essential to ecosystem function and distinguish among mutualism, commensalism, parasitism, and competition by identifying the defining benefit-harm relationship in each, with a supporting example from the chapter.

competency.competency_text: Analyses patterns of relationships between living organisms and their environments in terms of dependence on and response to each other.

assessment_items.visual_stimulus:
Relationship | Organism 1 effect | Organism 2 effect | Chapter example
Mutualism | Benefit | Benefit | Honeybee and flower
Commensalism | Benefit | No effect | Orchid on tree branch
Parasitism | Benefit | Harm | Tick on dog
Competition | Reduced access | Reduced access | Two plants competing for sunlight
assessment_items.question_text: Refer to the table provided. An orchid plant grows on the branch of a large tree, using it as a surface to access sunlight. The tree is unaffected. A student claims this is an example of mutualism. Use the table to evaluate this claim and identify the correct relationship type.

options.label: A
options.text: The claim is correct — the orchid benefits from sunlight and the tree benefits from the orchid's oxygen production.

options.label: B
options.text: The claim is incorrect — this is commensalism because only the orchid benefits while the tree is unaffected.

options.label: C
options.text: The claim is incorrect — this is competition because both organisms are using the same tree branch as a resource.

options.label: D
options.text: The claim is incorrect — this is parasitism because the orchid uses the tree's branch without the tree's benefit.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Reveals the misconception that any co-existing organisms that produce something useful automatically benefit each other — the student invents a benefit for the tree (oxygen) not stated in the scenario, collapsing commensalism into mutualism.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Shows confusion between commensalism and parasitism: the student interprets 'using without giving back' as harm, not recognising that no effect is different from harm.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Reveals a misapplication of competition: the student sees two organisms near the same resource and defaults to competition without checking whether there is genuine resource reduction for the tree.

MCQ.inclusivity: Providing the completed relationship table as a reference during the question (as the visual stimulus does here) is itself an inclusivity scaffold. Students who need additional support can be asked to highlight the row in the table that matches their reasoning before selecting an option.

assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can explain why decomposers are essential to ecosystem function and distinguish among mutualism, commensalism, parasitism, and competition by identifying the defining benefit-harm relationship in each, with a supporting example from the chapter.

assessment_items.question_text: A forest floor where decomposers are completely absent would look very different from a normal forest floor. Explain what would happen to nutrient cycling if decomposers were removed from the forest ecosystem, and state why this would eventually affect the producers in the same ecosystem.
expected_elements: States that without decomposers, dead plants and animals would not be broken down into simpler substances.
Explains that nutrients locked in dead organic matter would not be returned to the soil.
Connects reduced soil nutrients to reduced availability of nutrients for producers (plants).
Concludes that producers would be unable to grow effectively, disrupting the rest of the food web above them.

SCR.inclusivity: Students can be given a diagram showing a normal decomposition cycle with one step blanked out and asked to describe the consequence of the missing step rather than constructing the full explanation from scratch. Verbal responses accepted where written response is challenging.

assessment_items.question_text: In the 1980s, large-scale export of frog legs from India significantly reduced frog populations in agricultural regions. Which sequence correctly traces the cascade of consequences that followed this reduction?

options.label: A
options.text: Fewer frogs → fewer dragonflies → more mosquitoes → more disease in human populations.

options.label: B
options.text: Fewer frogs → increased agricultural pests → higher synthetic pesticide use → further environmental harm.

options.label: C
options.text: Fewer frogs → more available food for snakes → snake populations rise → eagle populations rise.

options.label: D
options.text: Fewer frogs → reduced decomposition in ponds → fewer nutrients in soil → reduced plant growth.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Reveals that the student can construct a plausible cascade but confuses the chapter's specific case with a different ecological scenario — mosquitoes and disease are not the chapter's traced consequence, indicating recall of a different context rather than the frog case study.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Shows the student is reasoning upward through the food web (what benefits from fewer frogs) rather than outward to the agricultural and pest-control consequences — a logical but chapter-incorrect chain.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Reveals confusion between frog function and decomposer function — the student incorrectly attributes decomposition and nutrient cycling to frogs rather than to decomposers, mixing up two different chapter sections.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who struggle with multi-step sequences can be given the four consequences on separate slips and asked to arrange them in order before selecting the matching option. This externalises the sequencing task.

assessment_items.question_text: In the two-pond study, a pond with fish showed higher seed production in nearby flowering plants compared to a pond without fish. Which statement best explains the indirect pathway responsible for this difference?

options.label: A
options.text: Fish ate dragonfly larvae, reducing dragonfly numbers, which allowed more bees and butterflies to survive, increasing pollination and seed production in nearby plants.

options.label: B
options.text: Fish ate the algae in the pond, allowing more sunlight to reach the water surface and warm the soil near the plants.

options.label: C
options.text: Fish directly pollinated the flowering plants near the pond, increasing seed production.

options.label: D
options.text: Fish improved water quality in the pond, which enriched the soil near the pond and allowed plants to produce more seeds.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Reveals a failure to understand indirect effects — the student collapses the multi-step chain into a single direct fish-to-plant link, the most common error when students encounter indirect ecological effects for the first time.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Shows the student attempting to construct a plausible abiotic pathway (water quality → soil enrichment) but substituting an invented mechanism for the chapter's documented biotic chain — a sign of partial understanding mixed with confabulation.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Reveals a tendency to reach for a sunlight-based explanation — common because sunlight is the most prominent abiotic component studied — without grounding the explanation in the chapter's actual dragonfly-pollinator chain.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students can be asked to draw the chain from fish to seed production with labelled arrows before selecting an answer. This externalises the indirect chain and reduces the cognitive load of holding multiple steps in working memory simultaneously.

assessment_items.question_text: A factory begins releasing pollutants into a pond, causing most of the aquatic plants to die. Using the cascade described in the chapter, trace at least four linked consequences that follow from this plant death, and identify one step in the chain that crosses from the aquatic system into a terrestrial or human system.
expected_elements: Identifies plant death as the initial disruption causing reduced oxygen production in the pond.
Traces the consequence that reduced oxygen leads to fish death or decline.
Connects fewer fish to a rise in insect or consumer populations.
Traces how increased insects spread to farmland, leading farmers to use synthetic pesticides.
Identifies at least one step that crosses from aquatic to terrestrial or human systems (e.g. insects moving from pond to farmland, or pesticide use in human agriculture).

SCR.inclusivity: Students can be given a blank chain template with four arrow-linked boxes and asked to fill in each box rather than write continuous prose. Annotating the boundary-crossing step in a different colour is equally valid as naming it in words.

assessment_items.question_text: The Green Revolution significantly increased food production in India but also led to long-term ecological costs. Which statement most accurately evaluates both the benefit and an ecological cost of the Green Revolution's farming practices?

options.label: A
options.text: The Green Revolution increased food production and also increased soil biodiversity through the use of synthetic fertilisers.

options.label: B
options.text: The Green Revolution increased food production but caused soil degradation, loss of soil microorganisms, and reduction of pollinators through monoculture.

options.label: C
options.text: The Green Revolution increased food production with no long-term ecological costs because synthetic fertilisers are absorbed by the soil without residue.

options.label: D
options.text: The Green Revolution reduced food production in the short term but improved ecosystem health over decades through increased crop diversity.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Reveals a reversal of the chapter's claim — the student has not registered that synthetic fertilisers reduce rather than increase soil biodiversity, possibly because 'fertiliser' is generally associated with growth and benefit.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Reveals the misconception that chemical inputs are absorbed and neutralised by the soil — a common prior belief that the chapter directly challenges through its description of soil degradation and pest resistance.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Shows a wholesale reversal of the chapter's historical account — the student inverts both the short-term food production outcome and the long-term ecological trajectory, suggesting the Green Revolution section was not engaged with.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students can be asked to underline the claim about food production and separately underline the ecological cost in their notes before selecting an answer, separating the two dimensions of the evaluation task.

assessment_items.question_text: The Sundarbans mangrove forest is threatened by deforestation, illegal hunting, and industrial pollution. A student argues that the Sundarbans can recover on its own if human activities simply stop. Which reasoning best evaluates this argument using the chapter's evidence?

options.label: A
options.text: The argument is correct only for aquatic ecosystems like the Sundarbans because water naturally cleanses pollutants over time.

options.label: B
options.text: The argument is fully correct — all natural ecosystems recover automatically once human interference ends, as ecosystem balance is self-regulating.

options.label: C
options.text: The argument is fully incorrect — human-made ecosystems like the Sundarbans always require ongoing human management to survive.

options.label: D
options.text: The argument is partially correct — ecosystem balance is dynamic and can shift after disruption, but the extent of recovery depends on how severely biotic and abiotic relationships have been damaged.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Reveals overgeneralisation of the chapter's concept of dynamic balance — the student reads 'dynamic balance' as meaning 'always returns to equilibrium', ignoring the chapter's evidence that severe disruption can prevent recovery.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Reveals a factual confusion: the student has misclassified the Sundarbans as a human-made ecosystem (like a fish pond or farm park) when the chapter presents it as a natural mangrove forest, conflating section 12.9 with 12.9.1.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Reveals a misconception that water ecosystems self-cleanse — a plausible-sounding but chapter-unsupported generalisation that misapplies the concept of natural cycles to industrial pollution.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students can be asked to identify one piece of evidence from the Sundarbans case study that supports or challenges the recovery argument before selecting an option, grounding the evaluation in text rather than intuition.

assessment_items.question_text: The chapter describes two cases of large-scale human disruption: deforestation and hunting in the Sundarbans, and the adoption of synthetic fertilisers and pesticides during the Green Revolution. Compare these two cases and evaluate which disruption is more likely to cause irreversible damage to ecosystem relationships, using specific evidence from both cases to support your argument.
look_for: Names a specific disrupted relationship in each case (e.g. deforestation removing mangrove habitat in the Sundarbans; monoculture reducing pollinator populations during the Green Revolution).
Uses the chapter's concept of cascading consequences to explain why each disruption has system-wide effects, not just local ones.
Constructs an explicit comparative judgement — which disruption is more likely to be irreversible — with a reason grounded in chapter evidence rather than general knowledge.
Engages with the concept of dynamic balance: recognises that some disruptions exceed the threshold at which the ecosystem can self-regulate.
Avoids restating facts alone — the response must connect evidence causally to the evaluative claim.

ECR.inclusivity: Students who find comparison difficult can be asked to complete two separate evidence boxes first — one for each case — and then write a single sentence connecting the two before drafting the full evaluation. Students may respond with annotated diagrams alongside prose where verbal expression is challenging.

assessment_items.visual_stimulus:
Disruption | Ecosystem affected | Biotic relationship disrupted | Abiotic component affected | Predicted cascade consequence | Can the ecosystem recover without intervention? (Yes / No / Depends) | Evidence for your answer
Large-scale deforestation in the Sundarbans | Mangrove forest | | | | | 
Widespread monoculture farming during the Green Revolution | Farmland ecosystem | | | | | 
Complete removal of frogs from an agricultural region | Agricultural land + nearby water bodies | | | | |
assessment_items.task: Three disruptions to ecosystems are shown in the table provided. For each disruption: (1) name the biotic relationship that is directly disrupted, (2) identify one abiotic component that is subsequently affected, (3) predict the cascade consequence that follows, (4) judge whether the ecosystem can recover without human intervention, and (5) state one piece of evidence from the chapter that supports your judgement.
assessment_items.scaffold: For each row, start by asking: what living relationship depends on what has been lost? Then ask: what non-living component is affected as a result? Then trace one further consequence. Finally, use something specific from the chapter — a case study, a named species, or a described outcome — as your evidence for the recovery judgement.
format_of_output: Completed table with all five columns filled for each of the three disruptions.
One sentence per row stating the evidence used for the recovery judgement.

OPEN_TASK.format_type: Classification or sorting task with justification
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: A structured table requiring classification of disruption consequences and recovery judgements with evidence is the most direct vehicle for the final stage LO, which asks students to evaluate — using real case evidence — how biotic and abiotic relationships are disrupted and the conditions under which recovery is possible.
OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: A complete response demonstrates that the student can simultaneously analyse patterns of biotic-abiotic dependence, trace cascading consequences across ecosystem types, and evaluate recovery capacity with evidence — the full operation named in the dissolution test.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The table's five columns are ordered to scaffold reasoning from identification (what is disrupted) through mechanism (abiotic effect and cascade) to evaluation (recovery judgement and evidence). A student who fills all five columns with causally connected entries is demonstrating the target cognitive operation; a student who fills columns 1–3 but defaults to 'Yes' or 'No' in column 4 without evidence is showing analysis without evaluation.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong responses: name specific biotic relationships (e.g. fish-dragonfly-pollinator chain, mangrove-soil stability link), connect a specific abiotic component to the biotic disruption causally, and ground recovery judgements in named chapter evidence (frog ban outcome, Sundarbans UNESCO status and threats, Green Revolution soil degradation data). Weak responses: list ecosystem components without tracing causal connections, use 'Yes' or 'No' in column 4 without any supporting evidence, or repeat the same generic consequence (e.g. 'animals will die') across all three rows.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: The table format reduces the writing burden while preserving the analytical demand — students who struggle with extended prose can demonstrate the same cognitive operation through well-chosen column entries. Students who need additional support can complete just one row fully and leave the others as annotated notes. Oral explanation of reasoning alongside the table is an equally valid demonstration.
